children: By Emese Bartha and Paulo Trevisani
U.S. Treasury yields lost steam after reaching multi-year highs on Monday as investors grapple with the prospect of rising borrowing costs amid volatility in energy markets.

The 10-year Treasury yield rose past 5% for the first time since October 2023, before stabilizing slightly lower. The move mirrored oil prices, which rallied nearly 5% in early trade before easing to a 1% gain Monday afternoon. The dollar followed, strengthening in the morning against major currencies, then cooling later in the day.
The 10-year German Bund yield hit another 15-year high of 3.538%.
Investors are worried that central banks can no longer ignore higher prices, and will eventually have to raise interest rates.

"The spike in energy prices...has caught everyone's attention, including, in our view, the attention of the central banks," Neuberger portfolio manager Joseph Purtell said. Monetary policymakers "now are in a position where they are no longer just looking through these energy price shocks," he said.

That prospect will be tested Wednesday when the Federal Reserve is widely expected to raise rates for the first time since 2023, potentially launching a cycle of rising interest rates. Chairman Kevin Warsh will be pressured to provide some clarity, despite his aversion to forward guidance

"A cautious message on inflation fighting could deepen the credibility discount on U.S. bonds," said Paolo Zanghieri, senior economist at Generali Investments. "A forceful inflation warning could fuel expectations of a hiking cycle and push short-end yields higher."
U.S. money markets priced a 93% probability that the Fed will hike rates by a quarter of a percent, according to LSEG.

"The repricing [in U.S. interest-rate expectations] has kept Treasury yields elevated and provided support to the greenback," said Wael Makarem, a financial markets strategist at Exness. "Beyond this week, markets are pricing in further tightening this year and the next."
Across the Atlantic, elevated oil prices continue to pose an inflationary threat for Europe, with Brent crude at $106 a barrel.

The European Central Bank raised interest rates last week, bringing the deposit rate to 2.50%--a level widely viewed as the upper bound of neutral policy. The central bank also revised up its inflation forecasts for 2027 and 2028, alongside higher GDP projections for 2026 and 2027.
Some forecasters still see an argument for another Fed hold, given the volatility of energy prices.

Simon Ballard, chief economist at First Abu Dhabi Bank, said in a note that "monetary policy is a relatively blunt tool for combating geopolitically fuelled inflation." He expects the Fed to "keep its powder dry this week and allow the macro data backdrop to evolve before risking a more restrictive monetary policy stance."
